DWIM on the Notation page

“Do what I mean”: select some music, press DWIM, and the page shows the other ways that music could have been written, best first, each with a small score and a Use this button. The Notation page (tools/notation.qmd) offers it; the engine is Chord Entry’s (ChordEntry.alternatives) and the panel is MelodyDwim (apps/shared/melody-dwim.js), shared with the Chord Entry page.

This file is the plan and the record: what works now, how it stays working long after a take, and what is still to build. Keep it up to date when DWIM changes.

Two kinds of DWIM

Kind Needs Examples Status
Re-reading a take the take’s log (every key down/up with its time, and the settings) staccato vs note + rest, triplets or not, swing or straight, eighth vs sixteenth grid, plainest vs as-released note ends, grace notes, pickup built
Re-writing what is written only the notes on the page enharmonic spelling (F♯ / G♭), a chord’s other names (C6 / Am7), tie vs dotted note, octave of a passage, meter (6/8 vs 3/4), key planned, below

Re-reading is the stronger kind: it goes back to how the music was played and reads it again, so it can recover things the first reading threw away (a note too short to keep, a triplet read as eighths). It can only work where the page still has the playing.

Re-reading a take, long after the take

On the Chord Entry page a take’s log lives only until the next take. Here it is kept with the chunk:

chunk.takes = [{ voice, log, bars, sig: [per-bar signature] }]
  • log is ChordEntry.take(...).log(): { v, cfg, events }. It is small (a few kilobytes for a page of music) and is saved with the piece (localStorage), so DWIM works after a reload, tomorrow, next month.
  • voice is the voice the take was written into (a take for voice 2 does not answer for voice 1).
  • bars is how many bars the take wrote, from the chunk’s first bar.
  • sig[b] is a signature of what the take wrote in bar b (its rhythm and pitches, NotationDoc.barSig).

When it still applies. DWIM compares each selected bar’s signature now with the one recorded. A bar that is unchanged is fully “the take’s”. A bar that was edited (a note moved, a rhythm pattern added) is reported: “Bar 3 was changed after the take: using a reading replaces your changes in that bar.” Using a reading is still allowed: it is your call. Bars outside the take (added later) cannot be re-read.

What survives what.

Operation What happens to the take
editing notes elsewhere in the chunk nothing; only the edited bars report a change
splitting the chunk on a bar line each half keeps the take, with its bars counted from where the half starts (from)
splitting inside a bar the take is kept by the first half only for its whole bars; the bar that was cut is reported as changed
merging two chunks both takes are kept, the second one’s bars shifted by the first chunk’s length
duplicating a chunk or a section the copy keeps the take: DWIM works on the copy too
a new take into the same bars and voice replaces the old one there
reading ABC or ChordPro in takes are not in ABC: they are dropped (the page says so)

Using a reading replaces only the selected bars of that voice (NotationDoc.replaceBars), puts the new signatures in the take, and keeps the take’s settings as they were: the next DWIM on those bars starts from the reading you chose (it is shown as “As written now”).

How the button works

  1. Select on the staff: click a note (that bar), or shift-click a second note (all the bars between).
  2. DWIM is enabled when the selection lies in one chunk and that chunk has a take for that voice.
  3. The DWIM panel opens with those bars; its own From / To boxes can widen or narrow the range.
  4. Each card: what the reading changes, why someone would mean it, its cost (lower is plainer; notes left out cost most), and Use this.

Takes come from Play it in time. Chords from a take have their own DWIM (below) and are not touched by melody readings.

Planned: DWIM without a take

These work on any music on the page, typed, pasted or played. Each is a list of candidates with a cost, in the same panel, so the user sees one DWIM, not several tools.

  1. Chords. Every chord played in (one a bar, or in a take) keeps the notes that were played (chord.midis). ChordEntry.analyse(midis, { all: true }) already returns every reading that fits (C6 / Am7, slash or not); DWIM on a chord lists them. Typed chords have no notes; for those, offer enharmonic names only (C♯m / D♭m).
  2. Spelling. A selected note or span: the other spelling of each note out of the key (F♯ / G♭), using ChordEntry.spellNotes with the chord of the bar, which is what Chord Entry does for takes. Needs a spelling override on the note (pitches hold MIDI numbers; add spell: { k: "Gb" } beside them).
  3. Rhythm, plainer. Without the playing, the written durations can still be re-read: a note and rest pair as one staccato note, a dotted note vs a tie, sixteenth pairs as eighths when the meter allows.
  4. Meter. A chunk’s rhythm read in another meter with the same length of bar (6/8 vs 3/4, 2/2 vs 4/4), scored by how many notes cross beats; useful after a take recorded in the wrong meter.
  5. Octave. A passage that sits far from the voice’s clef: one octave up or down.
  6. Key. The key guess (NotationDoc.guessKey) with its runners-up and their scores, so a doubtful key can be compared and chosen; still confirmed by the user.

Order of work: 1 (data is already there), 2, then 3–6 as they are wanted.

Tests

  • node tests/abc/notation-doc.test.js: takes kept through split, merge, duplicate; bar signatures; replaceBars.
  • node tests/abc/notation.cdp.js: a take recorded (synthetic events), saved, the page reloaded, DWIM run on a bar, a reading used.
